source.title: Gradient descent with momentum - to accelerate or to super-accelerate?
source.authors: Goran Nakerst; John Brennan; M. Haque

record.tranche_reason: The study trains neural networks with a modified momentum optimizer and reports test-set accuracy and loss, but it does not test any listed version's specific comparison or mechanism.
record.gate_note: The MNIST results report test-set performance for super-accelerated momentum; the paper says training curves were similar because there was little or no overfitting at these stages. The plotted values are not given numerically in the text. RMSProp results are for synthetic loss minimization, not held-out generalization.
record.test_reason: The study tests optimization speed under different momentum lookahead values, not any listed generalization claim. Its MNIST experiments compare non-adaptive momentum variants; its RMSProp experiments use synthetic objectives without held-out evaluation. Wilson et al. and Choi et al. appear only as context for adaptive versus non-adaptive methods.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that super-acceleration often speeds optimization, including on MNIST, while late performance can become insensitive to σ. They also identify shallow directions and nonlinear trapping as limitations and regard the adaptive-method and stochastic investigations as preliminary. They draw no conclusion testing the listed generalization claims.
record.recipe_differences: The study proposes evaluating gradients at a point several estimated steps ahead, rather than the usual one-step lookahead; its MNIST experiments use small networks and report test accuracy and loss during training.
record.method_sensitivity: σ changes optimization speed; in the reported MNIST runs, later accuracy or loss tends to become independent of σ. The effect is also described as depending on network architecture.

fits_no_version.finding: Larger momentum lookahead values accelerate improvement in MNIST test accuracy and loss during training. Late curves tend to converge across lookahead values, with σ ≥ 2 already merging by 400 full-batch steps.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Super-accelerated momentum can reach a given MNIST test performance sooner, without establishing better eventual held-out performance.

record.problems: The MNIST results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. The MNIST networks are small, the non-stochastic tests use fixed learning rate η = 0.5, and the stochastic exploration is described as cursory. The paper says training and test curves are very similar because there is little or no overfitting at these stages.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were left out. Synthetic optimization and RMSProp results concern loss minimization rather than held-out generalization.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected generalization and the contribution of local connectivity or initialization.
Adaptive versus SGD held-out performance under specified tuning budgets and recovery through broader tuning, weight decay, or optimizer switching.
Batch-size effects on held-out performance under matched epoch budgets and recipe adaptations. Separate full-batch and mini-batch demonstrations do not establish this comparison.
Dropout's effect on held-out error and its dependence on dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance ranking generalization gaps against other measures. Analysis of synthetic curvature and damping does not test this relation.
Accuracy after removing highly memorized examples compared with removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All judgments use the supplied text. States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because the rows measure a different comparison; this does not dispute the authors' reported optimization improvements.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width beyond interpolation and test error across width.
Convolutional versus fully connected image-classifier generalization.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD held-out performance, tuning scope, weight decay, switching, and language-model comparisons.
Large-batch generalization under epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout's effect on held-out error and its interaction with data augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other measures tracking the generalization gap.
Effect of removing memorized training examples on held-out accuracy.

rows.value: σ = 4 provides superior training compared to smaller values of σ; plotted test values are figure only.
rows.note: Authors state the test accuracy and loss improve with super-acceleration; the text gives no numerical values. Training curves are described as very similar to test curves, with little or no overfitting at these training stages.
rows.check: This is the proposed optimizer's performance comparison, not evidence for a listed version. The reported improvement concerns training speed measured through test curves. Section 4 also reports that curves for σ ≥ 2 merge by 400 steps; the value should include this qualification. Numerical figure values are unavailable in the supplied text.

rows.value: Larger σ allows rapid optimization; in the long-time limit, accuracy or loss tends to become independent of σ; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The text describes faster optimization and convergence of accuracy or loss across σ in the long-time limit, without numerical test values.
rows.check: Faster optimization and eventual convergence across σ do not measure any listed version. The original partial state therefore has no applicable claim referent. Three runs are shown, but no numerical uncertainty or test values are supplied.
